summary: Academic writing is argument with receipts. Every non-trivial claim ties to a source the reader can independently retrieve and verify.

facts.text: Academic writing is argument with receipts. Every non-trivial claim ties to a source the reader can independently retrieve and verify.
Parenthetical: "Working memory degrades under cognitive load (Smith, 2024)."
Narrative: "Smith (2024) found that working memory degrades under cognitive load."
Direct quotes require a page or paragraph number: "(Smith, 2024, p. 42)"

facets.title: 3. Signal phrases — integrating sources into prose

facts.text: Signal-phrase verbs carry stance:
Neutral: notes, states, reports, observes, describes, writes
Argumentative: argues, contends, claims, asserts, maintains
Evidence-based: found, demonstrated, showed, established, documented
Hedged: suggests, proposes, hypothesizes, speculates, implies
Critical: disputes, challenges, questions, complicates, refutes
"Studies show..." with no citation is pseudo-citation. Three repairs:
Name the source. "Studies show" → "Cowan (2010) and Baddeley (2012) showed".
Drop the unsupportable claim. If you cannot find a citation, you do not yet have evidence.
Mark it as your own argument. "I argue that..." is honest.
Primary - original research, raw data, firsthand accounts.
Secondary - analysis or interpretation of primary sources.
Tertiary - compilations of secondary sources. Wikipedia, encyclopedias.
DOI (Digital Object Identifier) - Format 10.xxxx/yyyy. Include as https://doi.org/10.xxxx/yyyy. Required by APA 7, IEEE.
ORCID - persistent identifier for an author.
arXiv ID - preprints in physics, CS, math.
Claim - the conclusion you want the reader to accept.
Grounds (data, evidence) - the facts that support the claim.
Warrant - the underlying principle that lets the grounds support the claim.
Backing - support for the warrant itself.
Qualifier - limits on the claim.
Rebuttal - counterclaims and exceptions acknowledged.
Field opening - the broad domain
Sub-area - the specific corner of the field
Active debate - the specific scholarly conversation
The gap - what is missing
Your contribution - what your work does
Abstract - a self-contained summary readable without the paper. 150–300 words.
Context / problem (1 sentence)
Method (1–2 sentences)
Results (2–3 sentences with the actual numbers)
Implication (1 sentence)
Introduction - the opening section of the paper proper. Reviews relevant prior work, identifies the gap, states the research question.
Pseudo-citation - "Studies show...", "research suggests..."
Quote-bombing - paragraph after paragraph of standalone quotations
Secondary cited as primary - citing a source without reading it
Style mixing - APA in-text with MLA works-cited entries
Missing DOIs - references with URLs that will rot
Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association, 7th ed. (2020).
The Chicago Manual of Style, 17th ed. (2017).
MLA Handbook, 9th ed. (2021).
IEEE Reference Guide (current).
ICMJE Recommendations (Vancouver style).
Toulmin, S. E. The Uses of Argument. Cambridge University Press, 1958.
Writing a literature review that needs to move from a broad field opening down to your specific contribution without losing the reader (the literature-review funnel).
